To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Hageman-Arrindell and the Jacobson-Truax methods are more likely to identify changes that are not clinically significant than the method developed by Jacobson and colleagues.

(1) the Hageman-Arrindell method of identifying clinically significant client changes is not a reliable method, and (2) the Jacobson-True score method of identifying clinically and reliably significant client changes can be used with confidence.

the three methods of identifying clinically significant client changes (i.e., Jacobson and Truax's method, Hageman and Aarindell's method, and our method) are all useful in that they provide information on the reliability and clinical significance of client changes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying reliable and clinically relevant changes in psychotherapy.
how to identify client changes in psychotherapy which are both reliable (i.e., real and not due to error) and clinically significant (i.e., meaningful and not due to chance).
the development of methods to identify reliable and significant client change in psychotherapy and the application of these methods in the analysis of client change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the methods of identifying reliable client changes are all based on the assumption that the client is a random variable and that the changes in client scores over time are due to the client's random variation and not the therapy.
the three methods are not interchangeable, and the choice of which to use should be guided by specific research and clinical objectives.
all three methods have their advantages and disadvantages and should be used with care. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2012 APA, all rights reserved)
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Hageman-Arrindell method is most appropriate for identifying reliable and/or clinically relevant change in a client population, whereas the Jacobson-Truax method is most appropriate when identifying reliable and/or relevant change in a single client.
the three methods of identifying changes are complementary and should be used together to identify client changes.
the three methods of identifying changes are useful for clinical practice and research and that graphs are a useful adjunct to each method.
The main takeaway from our work is that
graphs of client change are useful in identifying reliable and clinically important changes, but that the interpretation of such change is a more difficult task.
the use of overlaid graphs is an effective way to communicate reliable and clinically significant changes to clients and clinicians alike.

reliable change indices (RCI), reliable and clinically significant change (RCSC) and the Jacobson-Truax method of identifying reliable and/or clinically relevant client changes are all useful tools for identifying reliable and clinically meaningful client change.
